readme:
# Relative Fargues–Fontaine function theory, Part II

Build the classical function theory of the variable pi on the period annuli over an arbitrary perfect complete rank-one field of characteristic p. Starting with the parent roadmap’s ramified Witt rings, untilts and graded algebra, derive zeros, divisors, closed ideals, Galois descent and the schematic curve. Compare with existing geometric and adic constructions, and state the exact hypotheses at boundary radii and under coefficient extension.

This continuation imports the parent ramified Witt and period-ring carriers, primitive untilts and graded Proj. It adds the norm, zero, divisor, ideal and descent calculations needed for the absolute schematic curve over a general perfect field. Geometric curve classification remains owned by VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals. The full target statements, API outlines, tests, exact supplier requests and source-version corrections are in the companion reader document.

The build runs HF0–HF7, then HF9–HF10, then HF8 and HF11; interval bundle descent is needed by the positive-line reconstruction in HF8. Every stage is planned at target level, with the mathematical gaps recorded in the packet; none is represented as a formalised library.

stages.title: Gauss norms, Newton polygons and completed annuli
stages.description:
Compare the parent period annuli with completion of ramified Witt Laurent series. Establish the coefficient norm formulas at radii 0 and 1, weak-topology comparison, Legendre duality, Newton slope multiplicities, compact norm stabilization, injective restrictions, and the ramified change-of-coefficient-field formula.

Targets: Classical and relative period annuli: For S=Spa(F,O_F), identify the completion of B^b=A[1/pi,1/[varpi]] for the norms |sum_n[x_n]pi^n|_rho=sup_n |x_n| rho^n (0<rho<=1), and the separately defined norm |x|_0=q^(-v_pi(x)), with the parent interval ring after its radius conversion. The comparison preserves E-algebra operations, each interior norm, restrictions and Frobenius. For E=Q_p it is the upstream AdicSpaces Layer 6 ring B^I. If 1 belongs to I, E is given the discrete topology; if 1 does not belong to I, use its local-field topology. For rho=q^-r with 0<rho<1, the Banach E-norm is n_rho(x)=|x|_rho^(1/r), so n_rho(pi)=q^-1. At rho=0 use n_0=|.|_0. On a compact interval avoiding 1 take the maximum of these normalized endpoint norms; its topology is that of the original Gauss norms. The unnormalized Gauss norms are used for Newton calculus, not as E-homogeneous norms. Ramified Gauss norm calculus: On B^b each interior Gauss norm is multiplicative, nonarchimedean and independent of pi. It is characterized by |[a]|_rho=|a|, |pi|_rho=rho and multiplicativity. For x in A and k>=0 put N_k(x)=max_(0<=n<=k)|x_n|. Then N_k(x+y)<=max(N_k(x),N_k(y)), N_k(xy)<=max_(i+j=k)N_i(x)N_j(y), N_k(pi x)=N_(k-1)(x) with N_(-1)=0, and N_k(phi x)=N_k(x)^q. These estimates pass to the completions. For rho=q^(-r), v_r(phi x)=q v_(r/q)(x). Radial limits and coefficient topology: For x=sum[x_n]pi^n in B^b, the limits |x|_rho as rho approaches 0 from above and 1 from below recover respectively the pi-adic leading index and sup_n|x_n| in the precise rescalings v_r(x)/r -> v_pi(x) as r->infinity and v_r(x)->v_0(x):=inf_n v_F(x_n) as r->0. On A, every interior norm induces the imported weak topology, |.|_0 induces the pi-adic topology, and |.|_1 induces the [varpi]-adic topology; A is complete for all these norms. For mixed-characteristic E and epsilon near 1 but epsilon!=1, |[epsilon]-1|_1=1. Legendre transforms and Newton polygons: Import proper lower-semicontinuous EReal-valued convex functions and Fenchel–Moreau duality from OptimalTransport Layer 5. In the real dual pair specialize its conjugate P* by L(P)(r)=-P*(-r)=inf_x(P(x)+rx), so P(x)=sup_r(L(P)(r)-rx). The source slope is the negative geometric derivative. For nonzero x in B^b define Newt(x) as the lower closed convex hull of (n,v_F(x_n)); its transform is v_r(x). Specialize infimal convolution to these polygons; finite-slope multiplicity is horizontal length. This node owns the polygon and sign bridge, not general convex duality. Newton products and Jensen formula: For nonzero x,y in B^b, Newt(xy)=Newt(x) star Newt(y). Source slopes concatenate with horizontal multiplicity. For x=product_(i=1)^d(pi-[a_i]), all 0<|a_i|<1, the slopes are v_F(a_i), and v_r(x)=sum_i min(r,v_F(a_i)). In particular integrating the jumps of the one-sided derivatives recovers the change in v_r, the nonarchimedean Jensen identity. Completed annuli and faithful restriction: For nonempty I subset [0,1], B_I is the inverse limit of B_J over compact nonempty subintervals J of I. On compact [a,b] its topology is given by max(|.|_a,|.|_b); on a general interval it is complete and metrizable. A embeds as a closed subring. Every nonempty restriction B_I->B_J for J subset I is injective. When 0 belongs to I, B_I embeds in B_{0}=W_OE(F)[1/pi]. Newton data on completed annuli: For 0!=f in B_I, define v_r(f)=-log_q|f|_(q^-r) at positive radii in I and define its left and right derivatives by stabilization from any B^b-approximating sequence. Newt_I(f) is the closed polygon determined by the restriction of this concave function, truncated to the slopes corresponding to I. At an interior slope r the multiplicity is partial_left v_r(f)-partial_right v_r(f), a nonnegative integer. At an included endpoint use its one-sided convention, including vertical rays; at radius 1 a zero slope may accumulate. Uniform stabilization of approximating norms: If f_n in B^b converges to nonzero f in B_I, then for every compact J subset I there is N such that |f_n|_rho=|f|_rho for every rho in J and n>=N. Consequently Newt_J(f) is realized by a single element of B^b, and completed Newton products still obey infimal convolution. Directional rank-two Gauss valuations: At an interior r define the lexicographically ordered rank-two valuations f |-> (v_r(f),partial_right v_r(f)) and f |-> (v_r(f),-partial_left v_r(f)); use the compatible ordered-group sign convention from additive valuations. They are continuous valuations on B_I. They lie in Spa(B_I,O_E+B_I^{circ circ}) but in general not in Spa(B_I,B_I^circ). Coefficient extensions and radius rescaling: Let Eprime/E be finite with ramification index e and residue degree f, and suppose F contains its residue field. Put Eprime_0=W_OE(F_(q^f))[1/pi]. Then B_(E,I) completed-tensor_(Eprime_0) Eprime is canonically B_(Eprime,I^(1/e)), with pi prime on the right and phi prime=phi^f. For compact I the ordinary tensor already suffices. Interior norm formulas use the chosen normalization qprime=q^f; at rho=0 the transported norm is the appropriate [Eprime:E]-power, not literal equality. The unramified case keeps the underlying ring and changes Frobenius to phi^f.

stages.title: Boundary function theory and explicit models
stages.description:
Characterize extension to either boundary, identify the overconvergent field and Robba units, construct the Frobenius-stable positive subring and its bivector and crystalline descriptions, and prove the monomial, cyclotomic, equal-characteristic and Hahn-series comparison formulas with their exact norm rescalings.

Targets: Expansions at radius zero: If 0 belongs to I and 1 does not, every f in B_I has a unique expansion sum_(n>=n0)[x_n]pi^n with x_n in F and |x_n|rho^n->0 as n->infinity for every positive rho in I. Under the common injection into B, B_[0,1]=B^b and its power-bounded subring is A. In mixed characteristic no assertion of existence, uniqueness or additivity of arbitrary two-sided Teichmuller expansions is made for B or B-plus. Extension across either boundary: Let I be an interval of positive radii. If 0 is in its closure, f extends uniquely to B_(I union {0}) exactly when Newt_I(f) is bounded to the left in its horizontal coordinate, equivalently pi^N f is bounded near 0 for some N. If 1 is in its closure, f extends uniquely to B_(I union {1}) exactly when its Newton polygon is bounded below, equivalently lim_(rho->1)|f|_rho is finite. The latter limit always exists in [0,infinity]. Both conditions give B_[0,1]=B^b. They do not imply extension across a missing boundary separated from the closure of I. Newton criterion for units: For 1 not in I, a nonzero f in B_I is a unit exactly when Newt_I(f) has no finite slope corresponding to a radius of I. For 1 in I it must have only possible slope 0 at that boundary and a finite right derivative there. Units extend across each boundary in the closure of I. In particular B^times=(B^b)^times and R^times=(E-dagger)^times, where R=colim_(rho->0) B_(0,rho] and E-dagger=colim B_[0,rho]. Overconvergent field and Robba germs: Identify the imported overconvergent bounded ring and Robba ring with E-dagger and R in the preceding colimits, for general perfect F and either characteristic of E. E-dagger is a Henselian discretely valued field for v_pi, with residue field F and completion W_OE(F)[1/pi]. For finite L/F the extension E-dagger_L/E-dagger_F has degree [L:F]. For F the completed perfection of k((t)), compare with the completed perfected classical bounded and Robba rings using the inverted-radius convention. Positive period subrings: Inside B_I define B_I^plus as the closure of B^{b,plus}=A[1/pi]. For 0<rho<1 set B_rho^plus equal to the rho-norm completion of A[1/pi], and put B^plus=intersection_(rho>0) B_rho^plus inside B. If 0 belongs to I, B_I^plus=B^{b,plus}. If min I=rho>0, the underlying algebras B_I^plus, B_rho^plus, B_[rho,1)^plus and B_[rho,1]^plus agree, with the last topology generally strictly stronger. Newton characterization of positivity: A nonzero f belongs to B_rho^plus exactly when its extended Newton polygon over [rho,1] lies in the nonnegative vertical half-plane, equivalently it extends to radius 1 with |f|_1<=1. B^plus is the corresponding intersection over rho and is the largest subring of B_rho^plus on which phi is bijective: B^plus=intersection_(n>=0) phi^n(B_rho^plus). This agrees with the classical B_rig^plus notation after the specified comparison. Monomial completed-perfection model: Let k/F_q be perfect, F the completion of k((t^(1/p^infinity))), |t|=q^-1, T=[t]. Identify A with sums sum_(alpha>=0 in Z[1/p]) a_alpha T^alpha, a_alpha in W_OE(k), such that for every n and every real bound M only finitely many alpha<M have a_alpha nonzero modulo pi^n. This is the weak (pi,T)-adic completion of the perfected polynomial model, with coefficients already pi-adically complete. For interior rho=q^-r, |sum a_alpha T^alpha|_rho=sup_alpha q^(-r v_pi(a_alpha)-alpha). In B_I allow alpha in Z[1/p] and rational coefficients W_OE(k)[1/pi], requiring these terms to tend to zero off finite sets at each interior radius, with the extra boundary bounds. Perfected annulus towers and norm powers: For the monomial model set K0=W_OE(k)[1/pi] with |pi|=q^-1, and send X to T. With rho=q^-r and checkrho=q^(-1/r), |i(f)|_rho=||f||_checkrho^r, where ||.|| is the ordinary K0-Gauss norm. The completed direct limit of the annulus algebras under X->X^q, with transformed intervals and norms, is B_I. The dense initial Laurent algebra must invert both pi and X. In characteristic zero the annulus tower is finite etale; in equal characteristic p the q-power tower is radicial. Cyclotomic coordinates on period annuli: For E=Q_p (q=p), use the Frobenius lift Q(X)=(1+X)^q-1 and the embedding X->[1+t]-1. For an ordinary annulus radius s>q^(-q/(q-1)), write s=q^(-1/r), so the period radius is rho=q^-r<q^(-(q-1)/q). In this range ||f||_s=|i(f)|_rho^(1/r). The completed perfected cyclotomic tower identifies with B_I for I contained in that strict period-radius range. For a ramified coefficient field the detailed Newton slopes must use v_pi(p) and the p-Frobenius iteration; no unramified slope formula is asserted for arbitrary E. Equal-characteristic exchange of variables: For E=F_q((pi)), B_I is the ordinary Laurent annulus algebra with coefficient field F and variable pi, with precisely the source boundary conditions. More generally for perfect k and E0=k((u)), F0=k((v)), exchange the two indices of a doubly convergent Laurent expansion to identify O(D_E0^*) and O(D_F0^*) as Frechet k-algebras. The Gauss parameters r and 1/r are exchanged and their numerical norms differ by the corresponding r-th power. The associated adic spaces are the common locus Spa(k[[u,v]],k[[u,v]]) minus V(uv), viewed over either valued field. Hahn-series period rings: Let Gamma be a nonzero subgroup of R with p Gamma=Gamma and F=k((t^Gamma)) the Hahn field of well-ordered support. In A write sum_(alpha in Gamma_nonnegative) a_alpha T^alpha with a_alpha in W_OE(k), whose nonzero support modulo pi^n is well ordered for every n. For interior I, B_I uses coefficients in W_OE(k)[1/pi] and, for every rho in I and positive c, the exponents on which |a_alpha|_rho q^-alpha>=c form a well-ordered set. The topology and Gauss norms are given by these coefficient bounds. Endpoint radii require the additional boundedness conditions, not merely interior convergence. Ramified Witt covectors and bivectors: For a discrete F_q-algebra R, define the unipotent covectors CWu(R)=colim_V W_OE,n(R); full covectors allow a negative tail generating a nilpotent ideal. Put BW(R)=lim_V CW(R), and BW(O_F)=lim_(0!=a ideal O_F) BW(O_F/a). It is an O_E-module whose elements have unique formal coefficients sum_(n in Z)[a_n]pi^n with a_n in O_F and liminf_(n->-infinity) q^n v_F(a_n)>0. Summation embeds this module in B^plus. Addition is the limit of the ramified Witt addition polynomials with the required q-power twists. Radius-dependent crystalline period rings: Assume E=Q_p and rho in |F^times|, 0<rho<1. Let a_rho={x in O_F:|x|<=rho} and b_rho=ker(W(O_F)->O_F/a_rho). Define A_cris,rho as the p-adic completion of the divided power envelope of b_rho compatible with the canonical divided powers on (p); put B_cris,rho^plus=A_cris,rho[1/p]. It is the pro-final p-adic PD thickening computing degree-zero crystalline sections, not a terminal object among individual nilpotent thickenings. Crystalline and holomorphic invariant periods: For E=Q_p, B_(rho^p)^plus is contained in B_cris,rho^plus, which is contained in B_rho^plus. Consequently B^plus=intersection_(n>=0) phi^n(B_cris,rho^plus). For an isocrystal D over W(k)[1/p], k perfect embedded in F, and a nonzero t in B_cris,rho^plus with phi(t)=pt, the phi-fixed vectors in D tensor B^plus[1/t] and D tensor B_cris,rho^plus[1/t] coincide. The local boundary valuation quotient: In B^{b,plus}=A[1/pi], put p_boundary={x:v_0(x)>0}, with v_0(x)=inf_n v_F(x_n), and m_boundary={sum[x_n]pi^n: every v_F(x_n)>0}. Define barB=B^{b,plus}/p_boundary. It is a local domain with maximal ideal m_boundary/p_boundary and residue field W_OE(k_F)[1/pi]. Frobenius is bijective on it and the quotient map extends to B^plus.

stages.title: Primitive equations and the topology of classical points
stages.description:
Extend the parent primitive-untilt dictionary to all primitive degrees, general complete pi-adic algebras and Q-compatible inverse limits. Prove division, roots in degree-one quotients, the valued proximity metric, its completeness on bounded subsets, Lubin–Tate parametrization and continuity in the Berkovich spectrum.

Targets: Q-compatible inverse limits: For a pi-adically complete O_E-algebra R and Q in O_E[X] with Q(0)=0 and Q congruent to X^q modulo pi, let R^{flat,Q} be the set of sequences (x_n) with Q(x_(n+1))=x_n. Transport its perfect F_q-algebra structure from lim_(Frob_q) R/pi via reduction. Its zeroth projection is multiplicative for the monomial Q=X^q, but for a general Q it is not asserted to be an additive or multiplicative ring map. The construction is canonically independent of Q after passage to the common reduced inverse limit. Reduction invariance of the Q-limit: If J is a closed ideal of R and R is complete for (J,pi), then reduction induces a bijection R^{flat,Q}->(R/J)^{flat,Q}. In particular the preceding comparison with the perfection of R/pi is valid. For a perfect F_q-algebra S, the Q-Teichmuller map identifies S with the Q-compatible inverse limit of W_OE(S). Ramified Fontaine map for complete algebras: For pi-adically complete R as above construct theta_Q:W_OE(R^{flat,Q})->R using the Q-twisted Witt ghost polynomials and the compatible-coordinate limits. It commutes with continuous algebra maps and with the Q-change identification. If Frobenius on R/pi is surjective, theta_Q is surjective. For E=Q_p and Q=X^p this map equals Mathlib WittVector.fontaineTheta on the existing PreTilt carrier, after the canonical inverse-limit identification. No new p-typical theta or Tilt carrier is introduced. Principal kernel criterion for theta: Assume R is pi-torsion-free. If a=sum_n[a_n]pi^n lies in ker theta_Q and the zeroth untilt coordinate of a_0 is pi times a unit of R, then ker theta_Q=(a). If pi has a compatible system of Q-roots represented by varpi in R^{flat,Q}, the kernel is generated by [varpi]_Q-pi. These are algebraic kernel assertions, with the induced pi-adic quotient topology. Primitive equations of arbitrary degree: For a=sum_(n>=0)[a_n]pi^n in A define PrimitiveDegree(a,d) by a_0!=0, a_d a unit of O_F, and a_i in m_F for every i<d. Equivalently a is not divisible by pi and the reduction to W_OE(k_F) has pi-order d. Primitive equations form a graded multiplicative monoid, degree zero is A^times, and irreducible primitive means positive degree with no factorization into two positive-degree primitive equations. Degree-one equations and their untilts are imported from RF2. Weierstrass division at a degree-one untilt: Assume F algebraically closed and a primitive of degree 1. For D=A/(a), the imported untilt theorem identifies D with the valuation ring of an algebraically closed complete untilt C. Every element of D is theta([x]) for x in O_F, every element has an n-th root for n>=1, and theta([x])=theta([y]) implies v_F(x)=v_F(y). The ideal (a) has a generator [c]-pi. Every b in A has b=wa+[d], d in O_F; the remainder representative d is not unique. More generally b has a convergent a-adic expansion sum_(n>=0)[d_n]a^n. Primitive points and marked untilts: Let Y_cl be the set of irreducible primitive principal ideals of A. Its degree-one locus is canonically the parent classical-untilt point set. For a degree-one point y, the quotient A/p_y and its localization are O_(C_y) and C_y, and theta_y extends to B^b. Normalize v_y by v_y(theta_y([x]))=v_F(x); then v_y(pi)=v_F(a_0) for a degree-one generator. This normalization usually differs from the local-field normalization of E. Over algebraically closed F all degree-one residue fields are algebraically closed, and the cyclotomic polynomials split there. For the Q_p construction with F algebraically closed, spherical completeness of F implies spherical completeness of C_y. Valuative proximity of degree-one points: For degree-one points y,z with p_z=(a_z), define delta(y,z)=v_y(theta_y(a_z)) in [0,infinity], independent of the primitive generator. It is symmetric, equals infinity exactly on the diagonal, and satisfies delta(y,w)>=min(delta(y,z),delta(z,w)). Thus d(y,z)=q^(-delta(y,z)), with q^-infinity=0, is an ultrametric. For a_r={b in A:v_0(b)>=r}, delta(y,z) is the largest r with p_y+a_r=p_z+a_r; this equality identifies the corresponding truncated untilt valuation rings. Completeness of bounded primitive-point loci: For each R>0 let Y_le_R={degree-one y:v_y(pi)<=R}. This locus is complete for d=q^-delta, and y |-> v_y(pi) is continuous. No completeness of the whole union over R is inferred. Lubin–Tate primitive equations: For a Lubin–Tate polynomial Q with Q congruent pi X modulo X^2 and Q congruent X^q modulo pi, and 0!=epsilon in m_F, set u_epsilon=Q([epsilon^(1/q)]_Q)/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q=[epsilon]_Q/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q and y_epsilon=(u_epsilon). It is primitive of degree one, with reduction epsilon^(1-1/q). The formal Lubin–Tate group on m_F gives an E-Banach space V with pi acting by q-Frobenius. For E=Q_p and Q=(1+X)^p-1, u_epsilon=sum_(i=0)^(p-1)[(1+epsilon)^(i/p)]. Normalize |pi|_E=q^-1 and use ||epsilon||_V=1/v_F(epsilon) for epsilon!=0, with ||0||_V=0. Then ||pi dot epsilon||_V=q^-1||epsilon||_V; the ordinary absolute value |epsilon|_F would not be a homogeneous E-vector norm. Lubin–Tate parametrization and topology: For F algebraically closed, epsilon |-> y_epsilon induces a bijection (V minus {0})/O_E^times -> Y_degree1. Give the source quotient the valuative proximity sup_(a in O_E^times) v_F(epsilon_1-a dot epsilon_2), using ordinary subtraction in F after the formal scalar action. It is at least q/(q-1) times delta(y_1,y_2), and the bijection is a homeomorphism. Modding by pi^Z yields P_E(V) homeomorphic to Y_degree1/phi^Z. The induced isomorphism C_y->C_(phi^k y) scales the F-normalized valuation by q^k, not by 1. Metric and Berkovich topologies: Embed the degree-one classical points into the multiplicative seminorm spectrum of B^b by f |-> q^(-v_y(f)/v_y(pi)). Equip that spectrum with pointwise convergence and require restriction to E to be the fixed pi-adic norm. The induced topology on the degree-one locus equals its metric topology. Gauss points are normalized by v_r/r. The proof uses min(v_y(f),delta)=min(v_z(f),delta) for delta=delta(y,z), not the false lower bound v_y(f)-v_z(f)>=delta. Primitive points under totally ramified coefficient change: Let Eprime/E be finite separable and totally ramified and F algebraically closed. The determinant norm from A_Eprime to A_E sends a degree-one primitive equation to a degree-one primitive equation. Contraction gives Y_(Eprime),degree1->Y_E,degree1 with residue-field isomorphisms and fibres of cardinality [Eprime:E]. If the extension is Galois, each fibre is a Gal(Eprime/E)-torsor. The degree-one assertion concerns ramified Witt primitive degree, not multiplication of that degree by [Eprime:E].

stages.title: Geometric zeros and Weierstrass factorization
stages.description:
Over algebraically closed F, prove factorization of primitive equations into degree-one factors, extraction of linear zeros from Newton slopes, geometric compact principal ideal rings, convergent products near radius 0, and the exact divisor criterion for divisibility.

Targets: Factorization of primitive equations: If F is algebraically closed, every primitive a in A of degree d>=1 is a product of exactly d degree-one primitive elements. Equivalently a=u product_(i=1)^d([c_i]-pi), with u in A^times and 0<|c_i|<1. Thus irreducible primitive equations have degree one. Evaluation and closed primitive ideals: For degree-one y with ||y||=q^(-v_y(pi)) in I, evaluation theta_y extends continuously B_I->C_y, satisfies |theta_y(f)|<=|f|_(||y||), and has kernel m_y B_I. Multiplication by a primitive generator has closed image; division of an element in that image respects every compact annular norm. On B_I^plus use its corresponding primitive ideal. If lambda=v_y(pi) is not a slope of f in B^b, v_y(f)=v_lambda(f). A zero at every Newton slope: Assume F algebraically closed. For nonzero f in B_I and every positive source slope lambda of Newt_I(f), there is y in Y_I with v_y(pi)=lambda and f(y)=0. One can divide off a degree-one primitive equation for y in B_I. For finitely many slopes listed with multiplicity one can divide off the corresponding product; the remaining polygon deletes exactly those segments. Geometric compact annuli and principal ideals: Over algebraically closed F, compare the source compact interval ring with the imported geometric affinoid PID theorem whenever its endpoints define an annular affinoid. Extend the comparison to arbitrary compact I subset [0,1): I={0} and I={rho} with rho not in |F^times| give complete fields; every other I gives a PID with maximal spectrum Y_I. The integral subring {f in B_[0,rho]:v_pi(f)>=0}, 0<rho<1, is a PID with the extra maximal ideal (pi). Weierstrass products near radius zero: For a sequence 0!=z_i in m_F with z_i->0, define W=product_(i>=1)(1-[z_i]/pi). The product converges in B^plus, uniformly for every compact positive-radius interval. For a nonzero f in B_I whose radii approach 0, list all zeros below a fixed rho_0 with multiplicity and choose their linear generators pi-[z_i]. Then f=Wg with g in B_(I union {0}) and no zeros below rho_0. If f in B_(0,1], then g in B^b; if f in B^plus, then g in A[1/pi]. Locally finite divisors on period annuli: For I subset (0,1), define Div(Y_I) to be integer functions on the classical point set whose support meets Y_J in a finite set for every compact J subset I; Div^plus is its pointwise nonnegative submonoid. Restriction is coefficient restriction. For finite support use exactly the pinned TauCeti WeilDivisor carrier and its weightedDegree, via the canonical finite-support comparison. For nonzero f define div_I(f)(y)=ord_y(f), where ord_y is imported from the completed de Rham DVR. This divisor is locally finite and div(fg)=div(f)+div(g). Divisibility detected by zeros: For F algebraically closed and I subset (0,1), nonzero f,g in B_I satisfy f in g B_I iff div_I(f)>=div_I(g). Hence div induces an injective map (B_I minus {0})/B_I^times -> Div^plus(Y_I), and the Newton polygon is determined by the divisor up to an integral horizontal and real vertical translation. On a compact interval the divisor map is surjective.

stages.title: Descent of points and zeros over perfect fields
stages.description:
Descend primitive ideals from the completed algebraic closure using almost traces and unit cohomology. Classify finite-orbit points by marked finite-degree untilts; define weighted radii and prove the slope/zero formula and degree-independent normalized product estimates.

Targets: Almost traces and completed fixed fields: Let C=completion of an algebraic closure of the perfect rank-one field F and G_F=Gal(Fbar/F). For finite L/F, m_F is contained in Tr_(L/F)(O_L). Continuous cohomology satisfies m_F H^1(G_F,O_C)=0, H^1(G_F,m_C)=0 and H^1(G_F,1+m_C)=0. Moreover C^{G_F}=F and W_OE(O_C)^{G_F}=A_F. Vanishing for ramified Witt principal units: For U=1+W_OE(m_C), with the weak Witt topology, H^1_cont(G_F,U)=0. Set U_k=1+pi^k W_OE(m_C), k>=1. Then U=lim U/U_k, U/U_1=1+m_C and U_k/U_(k+1)=m_C. All maps have the quotient topologies, and the successive coboundary corrections converge in U. Descent of stable primitive ideals: If a primitive principal ideal of A_C is G_F-stable, it has a primitive generator in A_F. Normalize its residue-Witt image to pi^d; the ratio c_sigma=sigma(a)/a lies in U and is continuous, so a unit coboundary makes the generator invariant. Continuity uses |c_sigma-c_tau|_rho=|sigma(a)-tau(a)|_rho/|a|_rho, with a fixed nonzero denominator. Primitive points as finite Galois orbits: There is a surjection beta:Y_C^{G_F-finite}->Y_F whose fibres are exactly G_F-orbits. If y is represented by an irreducible primitive a, deg(y) equals the size of beta^-1(y). A finite G_F-orbit of a degree-one point is reduced, and its orbit product descends to an irreducible primitive equation. For a stabilizer G_L, products run over the coset set G_F/G_L; L/F need not be Galois. Points and finite-degree marked untilts: For y=(a) in Y_F of degree d, K_y=B_F^b/(a)=A_F[1/pi]/(a) is perfectoid over E, with an isometric embedding F->K_y^flat of degree d. Points of degree d classify such pairs (K,iota) up to continuous E-isomorphism compatible with iota, allowing a common rescaling to make iota isometric. If z above y has stabilizer G_L, then K_y=C_z^{G_L}, K_y^flat=L, C_z is the completed algebraic closure of K_y, and Gal(K_y^alg/K_y)=Gal(Fbar/L). The map A_F->O_(K_y) is surjective exactly for d=1. Radius and degree of a general primitive point: For an irreducible primitive a=sum[a_n]pi^n of degree d set ||y||=|a_0|^(1/d). This is independent of the primitive generator and equals |pi|_(K_y) with the F-normalized untilt valuation. Set Y_(F,I)={y:||y|| in I}. The point degree is [K_y^flat:F], not [K_y:E]. The Newton polygon of a is linear with source slope -log_q||y|| on [0,d], zero thereafter, and infinite on negative abscissae. Weighted Newton zero formula: For 0!=f in B_(F,I), its positive finite source slopes are lambda=-log_q||y|| at the zeros y in Y_(F,I); the multiplicity at lambda is sum_(||y||=q^-lambda) deg(y) ord_y(f). Evaluation extends B_(F,I)->K_y with norm bound |f(y)|<=|f|_(||y||) and kernel m_y B_(F,I). The de Rham completion at y agrees with the imported ramified completed local ring, and geometric pullback repeats the local order at each of the deg(y) conjugates. Degree-independent normalized primitive generators: If y_i in Y_F have ||y_i||->0, choose primitive generators a_i in A_F with a_i/pi^(deg y_i)->1 in B^plus. For a point of radius s, write its geometric factor product w=product_(j=1)^d(pi-[z_j]), all |z_j|=s. A descent unit u can be chosen with |u-1|_1<=s^(1/2); whenever s<rho<1, |uw/pi^d-1|_rho<=max(s^(1/2),s/rho). This estimate is independent of d. Weierstrass products over a perfect field: For an effective locally finite divisor D supported in Y_(0,rho0], there is W in B_F^plus with div(W)=D, obtained from the normalized generators a_i/pi^(deg y_i). For an effective divisor supported in Y_[rho0,1), there is a nonzero H in B_F with div(H)>=D, using factors 1-(1-a_i/[a_(i,0)])^i after listing the points with multiplicity. The second assertion supplies a divisor majorant and does not assert equality.

stages.title: Closed ideals and meromorphic functions
stages.description:
For every perfect F prove the compact field/PID dichotomy, classify closed ideals by locally finite effective divisors, prove half-open Bezoutness, produce nonclosed maximal ideals, identify meromorphic functions with Frac(B), and establish Galois invariants of B and B-plus.

Targets: Compact period rings over a perfect field: For perfect F and compact nonempty I subset [0,1), B_(F,I) is a complete valued field if I={0}, or if I={rho} with rho not in |F^times|^(1/infinity). Otherwise it is a PID and its maximal ideals are exactly m_y B_(F,I) for y in Y_(F,I). If 0 belongs to I and I!={0}, the subring with v_pi>=0 is a PID whose maximal ideals are those point ideals together with (pi). The spectrum in the second assertion is Spm(B_I), not Spm(B_(I minus {0})). General-field divisor criterion: For I subset (0,1) and nonzero f,g in B_(F,I), f belongs to g B_(F,I) iff ord_y(f)>=ord_y(g) for all y in Y_(F,I). Equality of the divisors is equivalent to f/g in B_(F,I)^times. Thus div embeds nonzero elements modulo units in Div^plus(Y_(F,I)). Closed ideals and effective divisors: For I subset (0,1), D |-> a_D={f in B_(F,I):ord_y(f)>=D(y) for every y}; this map is an order-reversing bijection from effective locally finite divisors to nonzero closed ideals. Its inverse takes the minimum local order attained by the ideal. In particular closed maximal ideals are exactly the classical points Y_(F,I). Under compact restriction a_D B_J is the compact principal ideal of D restricted to Y_J. Half-open Bezout theorem: For 0<rho<1, B_(0,rho] is Bezout and its nonzero closed ideals are exactly its nonzero principal ideals. More generally on any I subset (0,1), the ideal (f,g) is principal iff min(div f,div g) is principal. The Robba colimit is Bezout; its carrier and standard discrete-coefficient special cases remain imported from the parent and RD.0. A nonclosed maximal ideal of an open annulus: If I has a missing boundary and admits a sequence of classical points escaping every compact subinterval towards it, B_I can have maximal ideals that are not closed. Choose a nonzero holomorphic function vanishing on such a locally finite sequence and form the increasing union of the principal ideals obtained by deleting progressively more of its zero factors. This union is a proper ideal dense on each compact annulus; any maximal ideal containing it is nonclosed. Hence the closed-ideal classification does not classify all ideals of a noncompact annulus. Meromorphic functions on the period domain: For positive-radius I define M(Y_I)=lim_(compact J subset I) Frac(B_J) with transition maps induced by the injective ring restrictions. A compatible family is a meromorphic function. Extend the local DVR order to its fractions and set div(f)=sum_y ord_y(f)[y], a locally finite integral divisor. This agrees with the imported finite Weil divisor operations on every compact subinterval. Global fractions and divisors: M(Y)=Frac(B). The divisor map induces an injection M(Y)^times/B^times -> Div(Y), and B={f in M(Y):div(f)>=0}, including 0. For nonzero meromorphic f,g, div(f)>=div(g) iff f/g belongs to B. Galois invariants of holomorphic period rings: For C=completion of Fbar, B_C^{G_F}=B_F and (B_C^plus)^{G_F}=B_F^plus. The equalities preserve the induced Frechet topologies and all annular restrictions where defined.

stages.title: Frobenius eigenvectors, orbit divisors and products
stages.description:
Refine the imported eigenvector carriers by their Banach topology and coefficient changes. Prove homogeneous factoriality in the geometric case, injectivity and geometric surjectivity of the orbit-divisor map, construct positive and negative Weierstrass products, compare with Lubin–Tate logarithms, and prove the Banach fundamental exact sequence and its corrected interpolation ideal.

Targets: Banach topology of Frobenius eigenspaces: For integers d>=0,h>=1, refine the imported space B^{phi^h=pi^d}=(B^plus)^{phi^h=pi^d} by its Banach E_h-topology: restriction to any fixed compact fundamental radial interval defines an equivalent norm. For d>0 its map to barB^{phi^h=pi^d} is a topological isomorphism, with inverse obtained by lim_k pi^(-kd) phi^(kh)(x) from a lift of a quotient eigenvector. The degree-zero space is E_h, and negative eigenvalues have no nonzero vectors. The positive-eigenvector equality and carrier remain owned by RF3 and VB1. Coefficient and uniformizer transport of eigenvectors: Changing pi to pi-prime transports the eigenspace canonically after tensoring with the d-th tensor power of the E_h-line L={u in W_OE(Fqbar)[1/pi]:phi^h(u)pi=u pi-prime}. A chosen nonzero u gives multiplication by u^d. For an unramified extension E_n/E, scalar extension from E_h to E_(nh) identifies B_E^{phi_E^h=pi^d} with B_(E_n)^{phi_(E_n)^h=pi^(nd)}. For a finite separable extension E-prime/E of degree N and residue degree f, the coefficient-ring comparison followed by the uniformizer twist converts degree d to degree Nd. These identifications respect products and the eigenvector Banach topologies. Factoriality of the homogeneous monoid: Assume F algebraically closed. In the imported P=direct_sum_(d>=0) B^{phi=pi^d}, every nonzero positive-degree homogeneous element is a product of d degree-one elements, uniquely up to E-units and permutation of the associated point-orbits. Thus the multiplicative monoid of nonzero homogeneous elements modulo E^times is free on P_1 minus {0} modulo E^times. This does not assert that the whole ungraded ring P is a UFD. Weighted divisors modulo Frobenius: Let |Y|/phi^Z be the set of classical Frobenius orbits. Define Div(Y/phi^Z) as the imported finite Weil-divisor group on this orbit set, weighted by deg(y). Pullback repeats each orbit coefficient along all its translates and identifies this group with the phi-invariant locally finite divisors on Y. For any 0<rho<1 its weighted degree is the sum deg(y)D(y) over rho^q<||y||<=rho. No new copy of the finite Weil-divisor carrier or its degree map is introduced. Divisors of homogeneous eigenvectors: For nonzero x in P_d the zero divisor is phi-invariant, descends to an effective orbit divisor, and has weighted degree d. The map from nonzero homogeneous elements modulo E^times to effective orbit divisors is injective for every F. It is surjective when F is algebraically closed. For a general perfect F its possible failure of surjectivity is measured later by the degree-zero character class, not erased by extending scalars. Positive Frobenius products: For b in M_d={b in A minus pi A:b modulo W(m_F) equals pi^d}, d>=0, define Pi_plus(b)=product_(n>=0) phi^n(b)/pi^d. The product converges in B^plus, satisfies phi(Pi_plus(b))=pi^d Pi_plus(b)/b, and has divisor sum_(n>=0) phi^n(div b), with the geometric Frobenius action convention fixed in the reader. It is multiplicative in b. M_0 is the group of b congruent to 1 modulo W(m_F), and M_d/M_0 identifies with primitive degree-d ideals. Negative Frobenius product as a difference equation: Assume F algebraically closed. For nonzero b in B^{b,plus} with v_pi(b)=0, the solutions x in B^b to phi(x)=bx form an E-line. It has a generator in A minus pi A when b is in M_d. Its E^times-class is denoted Pi_minus(b); its divisor is sum_(n<0) phi^n(div b). This is a difference-equation construction and does not assert convergence of the naive unnormalized infinite negative product. Full Frobenius orbit products: Assume F algebraically closed. For b in M_d, Pi(b)=Pi_plus(b)Pi_minus(b), defined up to E^times, is a nonzero element of P_d and has divisor sum_(n in Z) phi^n(div b). It is multiplicative modulo E^times and invariant under the M_0 normalization equivalence. Thus any effective orbit divisor is represented by a homogeneous eigenvector. Orbit products and Lubin–Tate logarithms: For the Lubin–Tate primitive equation u_epsilon=Q([epsilon^(1/q)]_Q)/[epsilon^(1/q)]_Q, its full orbit product agrees up to E^times with log_LT([epsilon]_Q). The logarithm is the limit of pi^(-n)[pi^n]_LT on the open unit disc. Its product expansion is grouped by finite torsion levels; no unconditional ordering of individual torsion factors is asserted. In equal characteristic the logarithm and this identity require the all-local-field extension recorded in request R-LT. Fundamental exact sequence with finite jets: Assume F algebraically closed. Let y_1,...,y_d be degree-one points such that two points on the same Frobenius orbit are equal, allowing repetitions. Choose t_i in P_1 with zero orbit y_i. Evaluation gives a strict exact sequence of Banach E-spaces 0 -> E product_i t_i -> P_d -> B/(product_i m_(y_i)) -> 0. For E=Q_p and one point repeated d times, this is 0 -> Q_p t^d -> B^{phi=p^d} -> B_dR^+/Fil^d -> 0. Graded fibres and the corrected interpolation ideal: Under the same geometric hypotheses, for t in P_1 vanishing at y the graded quotient P/tP identifies with {f in K_y[T]:f(0) in E}. If y_1,...,y_d satisfy the orbit separation condition above, then {x in B:phi^n(x) belongs to product_i m_(y_i) for all n>=0} is the principal ideal generated by phi(product_i Pi_minus(a_i)), for primitive generators a_i. The unshifted negative-half product omits the n=0 zeros. Without orbit separation the divisor condition must instead use the pointwise supremum of all backward translates of the initial divisor.

stages.title: Dedekind charts and the schematic curve
stages.description:
Identify imported geometric Proj charts with the classical construction, obtain the almost-Euclidean degree and the Bezout-to-PID criterion, descend de Rham jets and positive eigenvectors, compute the general-field Dedekind chart class group, and prove regularity, degree-one generation, the weighted product formula and the completed-local-ring comparison for Proj(P).

Targets: Geometric Be chart and degree: For algebraically closed F and nonzero t in P_1, the imported chart D_+(t) is Spec(Be), where Be=(B[1/t])^{phi=1}=(P[1/t])_0. This identifies its closed points with the orbits outside div(t), and its completed local rings with B_dR,y^plus. The function nu(f)=-ord_infinity(f), f nonzero in Be, is a nonnegative integer, additive on products, and vanishes exactly on E^times. Be is Bezout, and the resulting minimum-degree argument proves it is a PID. The curve, its Picard group and geometric HN theory remain imported from VB2. For the geometric chart the source also supplies weak almost-Euclidean division: for a,b in Be, b nonzero, there are q,r with a=bq+r and either r=0 or nu(r)<=nu(b). This weak inequality alone is not used as a Euclidean-domain criterion. Continuous descent of de Rham jets: Let C be the completed algebraic closure of F and z a finite-orbit point above y with stabilizer G_L, identified by tilting with the absolute Galois group of K_y. The invariant ring (B_dR,z^plus)^{G_L} is B_dR,y^plus, and likewise for its finite jets. A finite-length B_dR,z^plus-module with continuous semilinear action has H^1_cont=0. Scalar extension gives an equivalence from finitely generated B_dR,y^plus-modules to finitely generated B_dR,z^plus-modules with semilinear G_L-action continuous on every finite jet; the inverse is fixed vectors. No higher-cohomology assertion is included. The perfectoid Tate–Sen estimates needed for effectivity are request R-TATE. Galois cohomology of positive eigenvectors: For d>=1 and a finite-dimensional continuous E-representation V of G_F, H^1_cont(G_F,P_(C,d) tensor_E V)=0. If V is nonzero, its H^0 is nonzero. Both statements are compatible with the Banach topologies and finite scalar extension. The assertion of a nonzero H^0 explicitly excludes V=0. Dedekind Be over a perfect field: For any perfect F and nonzero t in P_(F,1), Be_F=(B_F[1/t])^{phi=1} is a Dedekind domain with units E^times. Its maximal ideals correspond to classical Frobenius orbits outside div(t). If f is nonzero then Be_F/(f) is the finite product, over the zeros of f off t, of B_dR,y^plus/Fil^(ord_y f); in particular each completed maximal localization is B_dR,y^plus. Ideal classes and continuous characters: For the general-field chart Be_F, Cl(Be_F) is canonically isomorphic to Hom_cont(G_F,E^times). A nonzero ideal becomes principal over Be_C; if I Be_C=(f), the associated character is sigma(f)/f. This convention fixes the inverse in the construction back from a twisted invariant section. In particular the general chart need not be principal. Generation of P by degree one: For every perfect F the E-algebra P_F is generated by P_(F,1): Sym^d_E(P_(F,1)) -> P_(F,d) is surjective for every d>=0. Thus each homogeneous section is a finite sum of products of degree-one sections. It need not itself be a single product when F is not algebraically closed. The schematic curve over general F: The imported X_(F,E)=Proj(P_F) is a regular noetherian integral scheme of dimension one. Its closed points are |Y_F|/phi^Z, the completed local ring at [y] is B_dR,y^plus, and the weight deg([y])=deg(y) gives sum_x deg(x)ord_x(f)=0 for nonzero rational f and H^0(X,O_X)=E. This is completeness in the weighted-curve sense of Definition 5.1.3; no finite-type properness over E is asserted.

stages.title: The interval site and coherent modules
stages.description:
Prove endpoint splitting and Mayer–Vietoris for all intervals in [0,1]. On intervals avoiding 1 establish exact-square gluing, finite-projective bundle equivalence, Frechet–Stein structure, the coadmissible coherent-module description, and the bounded-fibre-rank criterion for finite presentation.

Targets: The period interval site: Objects are nonempty intervals I in [0,1], morphisms are inclusions, and a family of subintervals covers I if its union is I and every compact subinterval of I is covered by finitely many members. Restriction sends I to the imported ring B_I. Bundle and coherent-module categories below are confined to I avoiding 1, whereas the ring sheaf statement includes both endpoints. Additive endpoint splitting: For any interval I in [0,1], let I_plus be the convex hull of I union {1} and I_minus the convex hull of I union {0}. Inside B_I, B_I=B_(I_plus)+B_(I_minus). A convergent expansion into Laurent approximants can be split by nonnegative and negative pi-indices: the nonnegative-index pieces sum in B_(I_minus), while the negative-index pieces sum in B_(I_plus). This is a convergent decomposition, not a claim of unique Teichmuller expansions for every completed element. Mayer–Vietoris and acyclicity on intervals: For intervals I,J in [0,1] with nonempty intersection, 0 -> B_(I union J) -> B_I direct_sum B_J -> B_(I intersect J) -> 0 is exact, with last map (f,g) |-> f-g. Equivalently inside the intersection ring, B_(I union J)=B_I intersect B_J and B_(I intersect J)=B_I+B_J. The interval ring functor is a sheaf on the admissible site and H^1(I,O)=0. Period functions as a Frechet–Stein algebra: For I subset [0,1), choose an increasing compact exhaustion J_n. The Banach rings B_(J_n) are noetherian, their restriction maps are flat and have dense image, and B_I=lim_n B_(J_n) is a Frechet–Stein E-algebra in the imported ND.2 sense. Its coherent systems and coadmissible modules therefore have exact global sections and B_J tensor_(B_I) Gamma(M)=M_J. Generic Frechet–Stein algebras, coadmissibility and their Theorems A/B are imported, not defined again here. Bundles and coherent systems on intervals: For I subset [0,1), define Fib(Y_I) as the 2-limit over compact nonempty J subset I of finite projective B_J-modules, and Coh(Y_I) as the corresponding 2-limit of finitely generated B_J-modules. Each object includes isomorphisms M_J tensor_(B_J) B_K ≅ M_K for K subset J, satisfying the identity and triple-inclusion cocycle conditions; morphisms commute with these isomorphisms. The categories of modules at a fixed ring use the existing generic finite-projective and coherent-module infrastructure. Global sections of interval bundles: For I subset [0,1), Gamma: Fib(Y_I) -> finite-projective B_I-modules is an exact tensor equivalence, with inverse M |-> (M tensor_(B_I) B_J)_J. It commutes with restriction to compact intervals. For I=(0,rho], all these modules are finite free. The generic affine-scheme finite-projective/vector-bundle equivalence is existing work in current TauCetiRoadmap AlgebraicVectorBundles; the target here is the noncompact interval comparison. Coherent systems and bounded fibres: For I subset [0,1), Gamma identifies Coh(Y_I) with the coadmissible B_I-modules. Such a module is noncanonically M direct_sum product_(y in Y_I) N_y, where M is finite projective, N_y is a finitely generated torsion B_dR,y^plus-module, and the nonzero N_y have locally finite support on compact annuli. It is finitely presented over B_I iff the dimensions of all fibres over k(y) are uniformly bounded. The lengths of the torsion modules themselves need not be bounded. Matrix factorization with a surjective tangent map: For Banach E-algebras B_1,B_2 mapping to A and Z in GL_n(A), assume the bounded linear map (U,V) |-> U+ZVZ^-1 from M_n(B_1) direct_sum M_n(B_2) to M_n(A) is surjective. Then a neighborhood of 1 in GL_n(A) is contained in {X Z Y Z^-1:X in GL_n(B_1),Y in GL_n(B_2)}. Additive surjectivity B_1+B_2=A alone is not the tangent hypothesis for arbitrary Z. The neighborhood may depend on Z. Effective interval gluing of bundles and coherent systems: For I_1,I_2 subset [0,1) with nonempty intersection, restriction identifies Fib(Y_(I_1 union I_2)) with triples (E_1,E_2,iota), where iota is an isomorphism on the overlap. The same holds for Coh. Finite-projective gluing is the imported exact-square theorem applied after the analytic surjectivity condition has actually been established. This condition is not inferred from the ring Mayer–Vietoris sequence alone. Closed submodules on a half-open annulus: For R=B_(F,(0,rho]), 0<rho<1, and a submodule N of R^d, N is closed iff it is finite free; in that case its rank is at most d. This includes general perfect F, rather than only the discrete-coefficient case of RD.0 or the classical cyclotomic case in PadicHodgeTheory.

stages.title: Finite extensions and continuous module descent
stages.description:
For compact intervals in [0,1) with endpoints in the value group prove finite etaleness under finite F-extension with an almost trace estimate; establish completed-algebraic-closure invariants, effective continuous semilinear finite-free descent and its compatibility with interval bundles. Record why the boundary-1 assertion fails.

Targets: Finite etale extension of compact period annuli: Let L/F be finite (hence separable, since F is perfect), and let I be a compact interval in [0,1) with nonzero endpoints in |F^times|. Then B_(L,I) is finite etale of constant degree [L:F] over B_(F,I); for a Galois extension its automorphism group is Gal(L/F). For the spectral unit balls, [epsilon] B_(F,I)^circ is contained in Tr_(L/F)(B_(L,I)^circ) for every nonzero epsilon in m_F. At I={0} this is the unramified Witt-field extension. Moreover the spectral unit-ball extension is almost finite etale for the ideal generated by [m_F] in the coefficient integral ring. Its almost finite projectivity and almost vanishing cotangent complex are proved through the same root-refined discriminant estimates; this is stronger than the displayed trace inclusion. Completed algebraic-closure invariants on compact annuli: For the same compact intervals I, B_(C,I)^{G_F}=B_(F,I) as topological E-algebras, C=completion(Fbar). Restrictions to smaller such intervals commute with this equality. This extends the global invariant assertion to each compact Banach annulus, including the boundary-0 field. Effective continuous semilinear descent: For I compact in [0,1) with endpoints in the F-value group, extension of scalars gives an equivalence between finite free B_(F,I)-modules and finite free B_(C,I)-modules with continuous semilinear G_F-action; its inverse is fixed vectors and the canonical base-change map is an isomorphism. Continuity uses the Banach norm of the module. The necessary uniform matrix-cocycle corrections are the quantitative input in request R-TATE. Continuous descent of interval bundles: For every I subset [0,1), Fib(Y_(F,I)) is equivalent to bundles on Y_(C,I) with a semilinear G_F-action whose action on sections over every compact subinterval is continuous. The equivalence and fixed-vector inverse commute with interval restriction, tensor products and Frobenius. The compact descent theorem is applied through a cofinal exhaustion with endpoints in |F^times|. Why radius one is excluded from etale descent: The finite-etale and continuous module descent statements above are not extended to intervals containing 1. For B_(0,1]=B^plus[1/[varpi]], finite F-extension need not produce the asserted finite-etale annular algebra. Likewise Frobenius modules over B^plus fail the Galois descent satisfied over B. The positivity boundary quotient retains residue-field Frobenius information that global B-descent loses.

stages.title: Curve functoriality, ample lines and reconstruction
stages.description:
Identify rational functions and the ind-scheme Frobenius quotient. Prove separable coefficient change and finite Galois base-field covers, distinguish algebraic-closure base change from completion, identify positive Frobenius-line section algebras, and prove Runge approximation and reconstruction of the adic quotient from the scheme together with its Gauss norms.

Targets: Rational functions and the ind-scheme quotient: E(X_F)=Frac(B_F)^{phi=1}. For a nonempty open U, O_X(U) is the intersection of the nonnegative local valuation rings at the closed points of U inside this field. The natural phi-invariant map colim_(compact I subset (0,1)) Spec(B_I) -> X is universal for phi-invariant maps to schemes. Each Spec(B_I)->X is flat; for I=[rho_1,rho_2] with rho_1<=rho_2^q it is faithfully flat. The fpqc equivalence relation is the actual kernel pair over X, not an asserted disjoint union of Frobenius graphs. Separable coefficient change of the curve: Let E-prime/E be finite separable, and assume the residue constants of E-prime embed in F. Then X_(F,E) tensor_E E-prime is canonically X_(F,E-prime), and the projection is finite etale of degree [E-prime:E]. For the unramified part the underlying period ring is unchanged and Frobenius is iterated; for the totally ramified part use the completed tensor comparison and rescale radii by the ramification index. The generic printed identity B_(E-prime)=B_E tensor_E E-prime is not used in the unramified case. Finite extensions of the tilt give etale covers: For finite Galois L/F, X_(L,E)->X_(F,E) is finite etale Galois with group Gal(L/F), of degree [L:F]. Closed-point stabilizers act faithfully as Gal(K_z/K_y) on the corresponding residue fields, so inertia is trivial. Non-Galois finite separable extensions give finite etale maps by passage to a Galois closure. Curve of the uncompleted algebraic closure: Define X_(Fbar,E)=lim_(finite L/F in Fbar) X_(L,E) in schemes, with affine chart rings the filtered colimits of the finite-etale Dedekind chart rings. It is a regular noetherian curve with constant field E, despite the infinite tower. There are G_F-equivariant maps X_(C,E)->X_(Fbar,E)->X_(F,E), C=completion(Fbar). Finite-orbit points survive as closed points; a point of X_C with infinite G_F-orbit maps to the generic point of the tower curve. Finite-projective Frobenius modules on B: Specialize the existing finite-projective semilinear-module pattern of VB1 to the already imported ring B, not to its Robba germ. Objects are finite projective B-modules M with a semilinear Phi whose linearization phi^*M -> M is an isomorphism. Morphisms commute with Phi; tensor products and internal Homs carry the induced Frobenius, and H^0(M)=ker(Phi-1). By HF9 this is also the category of interval bundles on (0,1) with invertible Frobenius descent datum. No equivalence with Frobenius modules over the Robba germ is asserted here. Degree and characters of Frobenius lines: For a rank-one object (M,Phi), after extension to B_C choose a basis with Phi(e)=lambda e and define deg(M)=-v_pi(lambda). It is independent of basis and additive on tensor products. Degree maps Pic(phi-Mod_B) onto Z, and its kernel Pic^0 is canonically Hom_cont(G_F,E^times) via the action on geometric fixed vectors. The character statement is about degree zero; arbitrary-degree lines do not have a one-dimensional fixed-vector space. Every positive Frobenius line presents the same curve: For positive-degree Frobenius lines L_1,L_2, multiplication H^0(L_1) tensor_E H^0(L_2) -> H^0(L_1 tensor L_2) is surjective. For any positive-degree L its section algebra is generated in degree one and X≅Proj(direct_sum_(d>=0) H^0(L^tensor d)), canonically. In particular for lambda in B^times with v_pi(lambda)>0, X≅Proj(direct_sum_(d>=0) B^{phi=lambda^d}). Runge approximation and recovery of the adic curve: Let I be a compact interval in (0,1) with endpoints in |F^times| and I intersect I^q empty. If t in P_1 has no zeros on Y_I, Be_t is dense in B_I. The ringed scheme (X,O_X), together with all radial Gauss norms, recovers the adic Frobenius quotient. The bare E-scheme without these norms is not asserted to determine that adic space.

stages.title: Arithmetic examples and maximal completeness
stages.description:
Supply the strict-untilt and nonprincipal bounded-function examples, classify closed prime ideals of the integral period ring, and formulate maximal-completeness and automorphism-orbit results with the necessary valued homogeneity hypothesis. These discriminate the general-perfect-field theory from the geometric special case.

Targets: A nonprincipal ideal of B-plus: For E=Q_p and F=C_p^flat, choose a convex decreasing sequence beta_j in Z[1/p] tending to an irrational beta>0. With Y=[p^flat], put f=sum_(i>=0) p^i Y^(beta_(2i)) and g=sum_(i>=0) p^i Y^(beta_(2i+1)). The two-generated ideal (f,g) is not principal in A[1/p], and remains nonprincipal in B^plus. Thus B^plus is not Bezout in this example. This does not settle whether B itself is Bezout. A strict endomorphism of a completed algebraic closure: Let k be a perfect field of characteristic p and C_k a completed algebraic closure of k((t)). There is a continuous k-linear field endomorphism C_k->C_k which is not surjective. One may first adjoin algebraic residue constants inside C_k to run the explicit construction, so it does not require the given k itself to contain infinitely many algebraic constants. Untilts not topologically isomorphic to Cp: There is an algebraically closed perfectoid field K over Q_p with K^flat≅C_p^flat and K not isomorphic to C_p as a topological field. Consequently the Q_p-curve for C_p^flat has a degree-one closed point with residue field K; this point can be chosen away from the standard infinity point and hence appears as a maximal quotient of Be. No nonisomorphism of the underlying abstract fields is asserted. Closed prime ideals of the integral period ring: Assume F algebraically closed and E of mixed characteristic. For the weak topology on A=W_OE(O_F), the closed prime ideals are (0), the unique maximal ideal (pi)+W_OE(m_F), (pi), W_OE(m_F), and the primitive degree-one ideals (pi-[a]) for nonzero a in m_F modulo equality of ideals. Their residue fields are respectively Frac(A), k_F, F, W_OE(k_F)[1/pi], and the marked algebraically closed untilt K_a. Here residue field means Frac(A/p), not the quotient A/p in every case. Automorphism orbits under valued homogeneity: Let F be an algebraically closed perfect complete rank-one field and let Aut_top,Fq(F) act on it, allowing positive rescaling of the real valuation. Assume the valued homogeneity property that this group is transitive on m_F minus {0}. Then its action on the degree-one primitive point space is transitive, and for a chosen untilt K the closed orbit-point set of X is Aut_top,Fq(F)/(Aut_top,E(K) times phi^Z), with the stabilizer product interpreted through the marked tilting action. Maximal completeness alone is not substituted for this homogeneity property for arbitrary value groups. Higher eigenvectors and the boundary of representability: For E=Q_p the eigensheaf B^{phi=p^2} must not be modeled by an asserted unique two-sided Teichmuller parametrization in two F-coordinates. Its Banach–Colmez diamond description is imported from VB3, while the stronger assertion that it is not represented by an analytic/perfectoid space needs a separate obstruction. The sufficient representability range 0<lambda<=1 does not by itself prove failure at lambda=2.
